cues.text: Chapter two: Database design and the relational model.
Let's start with how a database gets designed.
Design begins with requirements and business rules.
From there, you move to conceptual ER modelling, then logical schema design, then normalisation.
After that comes physical design, which covers indexes, partitioning and storage.
Then implementation, then validation, and finally maintenance.
Three of these stages are worth separating clearly.
A conceptual model is technology-independent, so it says nothing about any particular database product.
Logical modelling converts relationships into tables and constraints.
Physical design selects the actual implementation details.
Now the building blocks of ER modelling.
An entity is a distinguishable object.
An attribute describes an entity.
A relationship connects entities.
Cardinality describes how many things on each side are associated, and the source names three kinds: one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many.
Optionality is a different idea: it states whether participation in a relationship is required.
And when you meet a many-to-many relationship, it becomes an associative table.
Let's make this concrete with an example.
VitalNet Health needs patient records and repeated clinical readings.
Here is the diagram.
A PATIENT has a one-to-many relationship with VISIT: one patient, many visits.
A VISIT in turn has a one-to-many relationship with OBSERVATION: one visit, many observations.
Then, reading the line beneath VISIT, many visits relate to one CLINIC, so each visit happens at one clinic, while a clinic can host many visits.
The last line shows PATIENT with a one-to-many relationship to PATIENT_ALLERGY, and PATIENT_ALLERGY has a many-to-one relationship with ALLERGY.
So patients and allergies are really many-to-many, and PATIENT_ALLERGY is the associative table sitting between them.
Now the relational vocabulary.
A relation is a table.
A tuple is a row.
An attribute is a column.
A domain is the set of valid values for an attribute.
Next, keys.
A superkey uniquely identifies rows.
A candidate key is a minimal superkey, meaning you can't remove any column from it and still have uniqueness.
The primary key is the candidate key you choose.
Alternate keys are the other candidate keys.
A foreign key references an eligible unique key in another table, or even in the same table.
A composite key uses multiple columns.
Three integrity rules go with these.
Entity integrity requires primary-key values to be unique and non-null.
Referential integrity prevents dangling references, that is, pointers to rows that don't exist.
Domain integrity constrains types and values.
Now the SQL, which implements the VitalNet design.
The source presents it as an example and doesn't say it was run, so treat it as an illustration of the structure.
First, the clinic table.
It has clinic_id, an integer and the primary key, and region, text, declared NOT NULL so every clinic must have a region.
Second, the patient table.
It has patient_id, an integer primary key, and patient_name, text, NOT NULL.
Third, the visit table.
It has visit_id as the integer primary key.
Then patient_id, an integer, NOT NULL, and it REFERENCES patient on patient_id, so every visit must belong to an existing patient.
Likewise clinic_id is NOT NULL and references clinic, so every visit must point to an existing clinic.
Finally visited_at is a timestamp with time zone, NOT NULL.

Fourth, the observation table. observation_id is the integer primary key. visit_id is NOT NULL and references visit, so each observation belongs to an existing visit. heart_rate is an integer with a CHECK that it is greater than zero.
And recorded_at is a timestamp with time zone, NOT NULL.
Last, a query.
It selects the patient name, the visit time and the heart rate.
It starts from patient, aliased p, joins visit, aliased v, USING patient_id, and then joins observation, aliased o, USING visit_id.
The purpose is to follow the foreign-key chain from patient to visit to observation, giving each heart-rate reading with who it belonged to and when the visit happened.
Now some important qualifications.
A CHECK permits NULL unless NOT NULL is also specified.
So in our table, heart_rate could still be NULL, because the greater-than-zero check only applies to actual values.
Similarly, a foreign key does not by itself require participation if it is nullable.
If the column can be NULL, a row may simply have no related row.
To model many-to-many associations, use a bridge table with a composite primary key.
Finally, two kinds of key.
A natural key comes from business data.
A surrogate key is generated independently.
And note that unique business identifiers can still require constraints even when surrogate keys are used, because the surrogate key alone doesn't stop duplicates in the real-world identifier.
